cues.text: A Childhood of Poverty
Born on October 16, 1890, in Corinaldo, in the Marche region of Italy, Maria Goretti was one of six children of the sharecropper Luigi Goretti and his wife Assunta.
In 1899 the family moved to Le Ferriere, near Nettuno south of Rome, to work land belonging to a local landowner, sharing their modest dwelling with another laboring family, the Serenellis.
When Luigi died of malaria the following year, Assunta was left to support the household alone.
Though barely ten, Maria took on running the home and caring for her younger siblings while her mother and older brothers labored in the fields.
A Household Under Strain
Among those sharing the Gorettis' house was Alessandro Serenelli , a young man of about twenty.
His behavior toward Maria grew increasingly threatening in the months before her death.
He repeatedly pressed unwanted advances on her, which she consistently refused, though she did not tell her mother, not wishing to cause trouble within the shared household.
We recognize in this quiet endurance something many children carry alone even now — a fear of burdening others that leaves real danger unspoken until it is too late.
"It Is a Sin"

On July 5, 1902, Alessandro attempted to force himself upon her; Maria resisted, crying out, according to the consistent testimony later given at his trial, that it was a sin and that God did not want it.
When she continued to refuse and threatened to expose him, Alessandro stabbed her repeatedly.
She was found gravely wounded and rushed to a hospital in Nettuno, where she underwent surgery without anesthetic, fully conscious throughout.
A Dying Forgiveness

Maria lingered for roughly twenty hours after the attack, during which, according to the consistent testimony of those present, she forgave her attacker and expressed her wish that he join her one day in Paradise.
She died on July 6, 1902, not yet twelve years old, having received Viaticum and the Anointing of the Sick shortly before her death.
Alessandro Serenelli was arrested, tried, and sentenced to thirty years' imprisonment.
A Prisoner's Conversion
For several years Alessandro remained unrepentant, but around 1910, tradition holds, he experienced a vivid dream.
Maria appeared to him offering lilies that burned away as he held them, marking, by his own later account, the beginning of a genuine and lasting conversion.
On his release after twenty-seven years, he traveled at once to seek out Assunta Goretti and beg her forgiveness in person.
She is remembered as having told him that if her own daughter could forgive him, she could withhold nothing herself.
Canonization
Maria Goretti was beatified on April 27, 1947, and canonized on June 24, 1950, both ceremonies performed by Pope Pius XII.
He honored her as "the Saint Agnes of the twentieth century."
Her mother Assunta, then in her eighties, was present at the canonization, along with four of Maria's surviving siblings.
It was the first time in the Church's history that a mother had witnessed her own child raised to the altars, before a crowd historians estimate at several hundred thousand.

Popular accounts describe Alessandro Serenelli, by then an elderly lay brother among the Capuchins, as present among the faithful that day as well, though biographers have not fully settled every detail of his attendance at either ceremony.
Legacy
Maria Goretti remains one of the youngest saints ever canonized by the Church, honored today as patroness of youth, of purity, and of victims of assault.
Her witness continues to speak two ways at once, and the Church has never let either half fall silent: to the courage of a child.
She chose death rather than consent to violence against her, and to the mercy that could, in time, transform even the man who took her life.
He became a penitent capable of receiving forgiveness he did not deserve and had not asked to be spared from earning.
